Announcing that the vehicle was a 1949 model, Rhinehardt let the screen door slam shut behind him. He navigated around dog waste on the lawn as he made his way to the burned-out Buick. The car's internal gears were heavily rusted, and its fenders drooped in a manner reminiscent of the slumped shoulders of a fired worker deprived of beer. 

Rhinehardt walked entirely around the automobile, kicking its tires and examining the front grille, which still trapped the winged remains of a sparrow. Peering into the cabin, he disturbed a cluster of flies that scattered into the air like beaten dust before gathering together again on the sun visor. 

After spitting and using his tongue to shift an artificial tooth back into position, Rhinehardt acknowledged that the other person was completely correct about it being a 1950 model, noting the absence of a running board. He shoved a one-dollar bill into his son's hand and went up onto the porch, where he snapped a towel at his wife to make her relinquish a chair. 

Sitting there as night approached, he gazed past the road toward a cluster of trees, where he pictured an airplane crashing down and erupting in flames—a eventuality he was willing to wager two dollars on.
outputs.L3:
The charred hulk of the Buick rested heavily in the overgrown grass of the yard. Rhinehardt walked a slow, deliberate circle around it, wiping sweat from his brow as he squinted at the melted chrome and blackened steel. At first glance, he was convinced it was a 1949 model—he recognized the heavy contours of the hood and the broad, sweeping lines. 

However, upon bending down for a closer inspection, his eyes caught the smooth side panel where an extra step ought to have been. There was no running board. Rhinehardt grunted, forced to admit that his son had been right all along. It was a 1950 model. Grudgingly acknowledging his defeat, he reached into his trousers, pulled out a crumpled dollar bill, and handed it over to the boy to settle their small wager.

Turning his back on the ruined car, Rhinehardt retreated toward the house to escape the stifling afternoon heat. As he stepped onto the porch, he found his wife occupying the comfortable wicker chair. Unwilling to ask her to move, he yanked a dish towel from his shoulder and snapped it aggressively in her direction. The sharp crack of the cloth startled her, successfully displacing her from the seat so he could claim it for himself.

As the sun dipped below the horizon and the stillness of night settled over the yard, Rhinehardt sat alone on the dark porch. In the distance, the faint, steady drone of an overhead airplane hummed through the evening air. Staring out past the silhouette of the burned Buick toward the dense treeline, a dark impulse crossed his mind. He leaned back in his stolen chair, quietly imagining what it would be like to lay down a two-dollar bet on the odds of the plane veering off course and plunging straight into the trees.
outputs.L4:
The sun baked the rust-caked weeds of the front yard, casting a harsh glare across the incinerated shell of the Buick. It sat like a beached whale of charred steel, its tires long melted into black sludge, its frame stripped by fire down to a ghostly skeleton. For Rhinehardt, the ruin wasn’t just an eyesore; it was an unpaid invoice, a point of pride, and the subject of a bitter ten-dollar wager.

He began his exhumation, walking a slow, deliberate circle around the carcass. The summer heat radiated off the scorched metal, carrying the faint, persistent stench of burnt foam and old damp ash. Rhinehardt squinted through the shimmer of heat, his calloused hands resting on his hips as he inspected the vehicle’s shattered geometry. 

First, he examined the front end. The iconic Buick grille—once a proud, toothy grin of polished chrome—was now a warped, melted grimace, blackened by the inferno that had gutted it. He leaned in close, peering through the empty sockets where the headlights had been, then shifted his attention to the cabin. Reaching through the open frame where a door used to be, he stroked the calcified remains of the dashboard. The gauges were fused into milky blobs of glass and wire, offering no clues, no registration tag, no serial plate intact enough to read.

It was all in the body lines. Rhinehardt stepped back, his eyes tracing the thick curve of the rear fender down to the rocker panels. He crouched in the dirt, wiping sweat from his brow, and dragged a finger along the lower seam beneath the doors. 

There was no ridge. No ledge. No step. 

The running board was completely absent—seamlessly integrated into the bodywork, a definitive styling shift that marked the dawn of a new decade.

“Nineteen-fifty,” Rhinehardt grunted to the empty air. 

He stood up, his knees popping like dry twigs, and looked toward the shaded patch of the driveway where his son, Jimmy, leaned against a battered pickup truck. Jimmy was smirking, arms crossed, knowing he had won before his father even spoke. Rhinehardt reached into his faded trousers, pulled out a wad of crumpled bills, and peeled off a sweat-stained ten-dollar note. He flicked it toward the boy without a word of congratulations. Jimmy caught it, stuffed it in his pocket, and sauntered off toward the road, the transaction completed with the cold efficiency of two strangers.

Left alone with the silence of the yard, Rhinehardt retreated from the oppressive sun. He climbed the sagging wooden steps of his porch and sank heavily into a rusting glider. The metal grooved beneath his weight, screeching a familiar, dull complaint. 

From the porch, the yard looked like a graveyard of forgotten machinery, dominated by the black hulk of the ’50 Buick. Rhinehardt tilted his head back against the frayed cushion and stared up at the pale, empty blue of the sky. 

A high-altitude jet cut a thin, white scar across the heavens, drifting silently eastward. 

Rhinehardt’s eyes narrowed as he watched the vapor trail. He imagined the twin engines sputtering, a flame licking the wing, the sudden, terrible pitch into an unrecoverable dive. He wondered what kind of odds he could get on a mid-air disaster. Two-to-one on an engine failure? Five-to-one on total loss of life? He ran the numbers in his head, mentally laying down bills he didn't have on a fiery plunge into the pine trees five miles out. 

He closed his eyes, listening to the hum of insects in the tall grass, wrapped completely in the comforting, familiar decay of his life—a life measured out in small losses, ruined metal, and the endless, dark itch for one more violent gamble.
outputs.L5:
In the quiet, slow-moving town of Oakridge, some things were considered immutable: the sound of the church bell at noon, the autumn chill in late October, and **Rhinehardt** behind the wheel of **the Buick**.

It wasn’t just *any* car; to the locals, it was spoken of with a soft, reverent emphasis: *The* Buick. A 1953 Roadmaster in two-tone midnight blue and shell white, the automobile possessed a grand authority that modern cars could never hope to match. It was a rolling temple of heavy American steel, sweeping chrome, and sweeping curves, powered by a V8 engine that purred with the steady, reassuring heartbeat of a bygone era.

Old man Rhinehardt had bought it brand new off the showroom floor the year he married his high school sweetheart, Martha. Over the decades, while the world around them accelerated—while gravel roads were paved over, gas stations changed hands, and neon gave way to digital screens—Rhinehardt and the Buick remained an unbroken link to the past. 

Every Saturday morning, rain or shine, Rhinehardt could be found in his driveway with a soft flannel rag in hand. He would meticulously polish the vehicle's famous portholes and glittering grille until they reflected the blue sky above. He didn't drive it far these days—just down to the local diner for coffee, over the ridge to visit Martha’s resting place, and back home. Yet, whenever he pulled the heavy chrome handle and stepped inside, the years seemed to melt away. Surrounded by the scent of aged leather and vintage wax, Rhinehardt wasn't an octogenarian with aching joints; he was twenty-two again, full of hope, with a lifetime of open road ahead.

Over the years, wealthy collectors often drifted into town, waving fat envelopes of cash and begging Rhinehardt to sell. They saw a pristine classic, a museum piece, or a profitable investment. But Rhinehardt always offered the same polite shake of his head and turned them away. 

To Rhinehardt, the Buick wasn't merely a machine. It was a vault of memories, keeping safe the echoes of laughter, summer road trips, and the quiet dignity of a life well-lived. As long as the key turned in the ignition and Rhinehardt held the wheel, the best parts of his history were never truly lost.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty narrative poem in the style of Philip Levine or Larry Levis about a working-class man inspecting a fire-damaged car in his yard.
counterfactuals.output:
It smells of burned insulation and the cold rain
that fell two nights ago into the ruined lap
of an eighty-eight LeSabre.
My thumb presses the blistered enamel on the hood—
it flakes away like black snow, exposing
the dull, unpolished slate of steel underneath.

Inside, the steering wheel is stripped down
to its thin skeleton of iron,
the cheap gray foam my palms smoothed smooth
over ten years of third-shift commutes
gone into a thick, poisonous smoke
that settled over the cabbage patch and the neighbour's fence.

It went up at two in the morning.
A short in the dash, maybe, or a dry fuel line
spitting onto the manifold.
I stood on the back porch in my work boots and undershirt,
a warm beer going flat in my hand,
watching the yellow light leap against the siding.
By the time the volunteer sirens began their long, sick whining
from down near the river,
the headliner had dropped like a burning web,
and the vinyl seats were already a black soup in the floorboards.

Now I kick a hunk of fused tail-light—
red plastic cooled into the shape of an old wound—
and listen to the dry weeds rustle against the quarter panel.
The engine block sits heavy in the grease-soaked dirt.
Cast iron doesn't care about fire.
It just turns red, then gray, then stubborn again,
waiting for someone with a chain and an old pickup
to drag it down to the yard off Route 4,
where they pay twelve dollars a ton for the bones of things.

My father used to say metal remembers where it came from.
He had thirty years at the forge in Wyandotte,
and grease driven so deep into the lines of his knuckles
that even the undertaker couldn't scrub it clean.
*Everything wants to be rust,* he told me once,
watching a rusted-out Ford sink into the clover.
*Fire just saves the wet air the trouble.*

I reach into the black cave where the glove box used to be
and pull out the frame of my sunglasses,
twisted like a copper wire,
and a handful of wet ash that used to be the title.
The wind comes up off the gravel pit,
carrying the scent of wet slag and dead goldenrod.
I don't wipe my hands on my pants.
I just stand there in the pale Michigan light,
bare-headed, forty-two years old,
holding a piece of cold slag,
feeling the sharp, familiar bite of the winter
settling into the iron of my back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that includes the following elements: a character named Rhinehardt, a burnt-out Buick, an argument about whether it's a '49 or a '50 model, paying a dollar to his son, and a dark ending involving a plane crash.
counterfactuals.output:
Rhinehardt kicked a wheel of melted slag,
Beside the scorched frame of a twisted ghost—
A burnt-out Buick draped in weed and rag,
Its rusted iron fried from coast to coast.

"She’s a forty-nine," he spat into the dust,
Pointing at the fender’s ruined seam.
"Fifty," said his son, squinting through the rust,
"The sweepline dips right there—it’s not a dream."

Old Rhinehardt grumbled, pulled a crumpled note,
A single dollar paid to settle the score.
His son took the cash and tucked it in his coat,
As overhead there came a deafening roar.

No storm was brewing in the dusk ahead;
A giant airliner had lost a wing.
It sheared the clouds in trailing streaks of red,
A screaming, plummeting, ruined thing.

It struck the open field in which they stood,
Consuming father, son, and burnt-out car.
The dollar scorched along with flesh and wood,
Beneath a sky devoid of any star.

Now twice the wreckage smoldered in the deep,
As ash settled where the wild weeds grew—
A sudden violence taking them to sleep,
Before the metal embers turned to blue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem about a guy who realizes he's wrong about the model year of an old junked car because it doesn't have a running board.
counterfactuals.output:
Deep in the brush behind the barn,
Half-drowned in grass and goldenrod,
I found the shell of an old sedan,
A rusted ghost in the quiet sod.

I brushed the brambles from the hood
And declared out loud to the open air,
"A thirty-five! I’d know that shape,
The way the steel sags over there."

I leaned right in to check the dash,
And went to rest my heavy boot
Where the running board was bound to be,
Above a thick, decaying root.

My foot dropped down through empty brush,
It found no ledge, no iron step,
No sturdy shelf of rubbered steel
Where drivers’ muddy boots had crept.

I pulled back slow and looked again
Along the rocker’s rusted line—
The fender swept right down the door,
A smooth and integrated sign.

No running board. The body widened out.
The side was modern, slick, and flat.
They didn't drop that step till late—
A thirty-five could not do that!

The streamlining had just begun;
The style had shifted down the track.
It wasn't mid-decade at all—
It had to be a forty-one.

I laughed out loud in the quiet woods,
My pride knocked down a year or ten.
It takes a simple missing step
To make a wise man think again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, cinematic poem capturing rural decay and suppressed hostility. Focus on a cynical man who sits on his porch at dusk after looking at a ruined car, secretly hoping to see a disaster on the horizon.
counterfactuals.output:
The sedan sits drowned in the chicory and brush,
A iron carcass stripped down to the bone.
Its spiderwebbed windshield drinks the dying sun,
Twin dead-eye headlights choked by overgrown stone.
He runs a dark thumb down the hood’s flaking scab,
Cold, oxidized red on a ghost of a frame—
Just another dead thing that the valley consumed
Without ever bothering to remember its name.

He walks to the porch where the pine floorboards groan,
A slow, heavy tread full of old, sour hate.
He sinks in the rocker with the splintered armrest
As twilight bleeds out on the edge of the state.
The air smells of creosote, dry rot, and dust,
The locusts sing sharp, like a saw hitting nail,
While the power lines hum over forgotten fields,
And the shadow of evening stretches long, thin, and pale.

His jaw stays clamped tight, a hard anvil of stone,
His knuckles still stained with black oil and grease.
He loathes the small lights turning on in the gap,
The fake, quiet town and its miserable peace.
He harbors a malice that thrives in the dark,
A cold, heavy violence that sits in his chest—
A wish that the rot spreading under his boots
Would swallow the east and consume all the west.

He stares past the silos, toward the curve of the ridge,
Where the interstate cuts like an open, black vein.
He waits for the flash. He prays for the tear.
A fiery collision. A derailed train.
Let a chemical bloom paint the twilight in red,
Let a pillar of smoke turn the evening to night.
He rests his dark hands on the arm of the chair,
Just waiting for the world to go up in light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: A poem about an old burnt Buick.
counterfactuals.output:
It slumps where weeds and thistles grow,
A charred and hollowed dynamo.
Once two-plus tons of polished steel,
A rolling throne, a heavy wheel—
Now reduced to ash and skin:
An old LeSabre, gutted in.

It used to hum with violent grace,
A king of time, a ghost of space,
With three chrome portholes on the side
That heralded a highway ride.
In cherry red or midnight navy,
The ride was smooth, the frame was heavy.

Until the night the dark spark caught,
And ruined what the factory wrought.
The flames licked up the velvet dash,
And turned the bench seats into ash.
The windshield melted, weeping tears
Of pooling glass for bygone years.

The steering wheel: a ring of wire.
The white-wall tires: fed to the fire.
The Dynaflow and engine block,
Fused together, dead as rock.
The smell of oil and burnt-out leather
Left to rot in open weather.

Now rust inherits what remains,
Washing away the scorch marks' stains.
A field mouse nests behind the grill,
The ghost of horsepower standing still.

A soot-stained monument of pride,
With nowhere left to take a ride,
It sleeps beneath the quiet sky
And watches faster worlds drive by.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
